name: MongoDB
summary: A document database server whose collections and indexes are persisted through storage-engine record stores, coordinated with replication and oplog state, and optionally partitioned behind sharded routing services.

features.name: Document and collection data model
features.description: MongoDB exposes database collections containing BSON documents and indexes; the server's collection and index abstractions sit above storage-engine record and cursor interfaces.
benefits: Lets indexes and query execution specialize around document fields
costs: Schema discipline and index selection remain application and operational concerns
Document and index representations can create write and storage amplification

features.name: Storage-engine record-store boundary
features.description: The server uses a storage-engine abstraction for record stores, recovery units, cursors, and write units of work; the fixed source includes a WiredTiger implementation beneath those server interfaces.
benefits: Separates collection/catalog behavior from physical storage implementation
Provides a transaction and recovery-unit boundary for storage operations
costs: Engine capabilities and durability semantics constrain higher layers
Abstraction crossings add coordination and implementation complexity

features.name: Replica-set oplog replication
features.description: MongoDB's replication source contains replica-set coordination and oplog-related components that represent primary writes, secondary application, rollback, and replication state transitions.
benefits: Provides redundant copies and failover-oriented topology
Separates replicated operation history from the local storage representation
costs: Replication lag, elections, rollback, and write concerns affect observed behavior
Keeping operation history and data state aligned adds recovery machinery

features.name: Sharded routing and ownership boundary
features.description: The source contains router and shard topology components that coordinate requests across shards, shard versions, migrations, and ownership metadata.
benefits: Scales collections across independent shard storage boundaries
Allows routing to use ownership metadata rather than broadcasting every operation
costs: Metadata refresh, migration, and multi-shard operations add coordination cost
Query and consistency behavior depends on shard-key and topology choices

mathematical_views.question: How do document and index operations refine into record-store, cursor, recovery-unit, and write-unit transitions?
assumptions: BSON documents and index entries are modeled as logical objects
The storage engine preserves the server-visible record contract at transaction boundaries
Physical page and cache behavior is outside the semantic view

mathematical_views.question: Which primary operation-history and secondary-application states preserve a replica set's replicated data contract?
assumptions: The oplog is modeled as an ordered operation history
Election, rollback, and lag are explicit transitions
Write acknowledgement policy is distinguished from eventual secondary application

mathematical_views.question: Which shard ownership metadata and routing transitions determine the set of nodes that may serve a request?
assumptions: A shard key maps a request to an ownership interval or set
Migration metadata is versioned and may be refreshed
Cross-shard transaction behavior is modeled separately from single-shard routing

costs: Schema and index governance remain operational work
Engine and recovery contracts add coordination complexity
Lag, election, rollback, and acknowledgement trade-offs
Migrations and multi-shard coordination increase complexity
